faq: How is a starter kit different from a template?
A template is a finished look. A starter kit is the working foundation, like sign in, database and deployment, without a design, so your developers can build your own product on it.
Can I choose a different stack?
Yes. We can work with React, Next.js, Astro, Node.js, Python and PostgreSQL or MongoDB. Tell us your stack in the order form and we confirm what we can set up.
Do I own the starter kit?
Yes. The repository is created in your own account and you can use it for as many projects as you like. We keep no rights to it.
Is it ready for real users?
It follows common good practice for security and structure, but it is a starting point, not a finished product. You or your developers still add the features that make it yours.
desc:
Production ready starter kits give a new project a clean base: framework, styling, sign in, database and deployment, already working together. Ecom Swift LLC assembles the starter around your chosen stack and hands over a documented repository your developers can clone the same day.

## What is a production ready starter kit?

A starter kit is a repository you copy to begin a new project. It is not a finished product. It holds the groundwork that every project repeats: a framework such as Next.js with TypeScript, a styling system, linting rules, a database with migrations, authentication, environment settings and a deployment route. Because all of these are chosen, connected and tested, your team starts on features instead of setup.

## Why the first days of a project matter so much

The first decisions in a project shape everything after them. A folder structure with no logic, mismatched library versions and missing formatting rules cause friction for months. Setup work is also repetitive and easy to get subtly wrong, such as an environment variable that works locally and fails on the server.

A starter that has been wired and tested removes that risk. Every developer who joins finds the same structure, the same commands and the same README. Nobody has to ask where the config lives.

## How a starter kit affects speed and quality

The most direct effect is time. Setup that might take a developer a few days of reading documentation and fixing conflicts becomes a clone, an install and a start command. That time goes into features that customers actually see.

Quality benefits too. Linting, formatting and tests catch mistakes before review. A pipeline that runs checks on every change keeps the main branch healthy. And because you own the repository, you can change anything. There is no hidden framework to work around.

## What a great starter kit includes

- A framework project with TypeScript and a sensible folder structure.
- Styling configured, such as Tailwind, with a few base components.
- Linting and formatting rules that run automatically.
- A database connection with migration tooling.
- Email sign in connected to the database.
- Three example screens that show how pages, components and data fit together.
- Environment variables documented and loaded safely, with an example file.
- Payment and email starters, such as Stripe checkout and transactional mail, where included.
- Automated tests and a continuous integration pipeline, where included.
- A README that takes a new developer from clone to running app.

## What we do

You tell us your preferred stack and the pieces you want inside. We assemble them, resolve version conflicts, deploy a preview and write the documentation. The Basic package is a clean repository with styling, rules and a preview deployment. Standard adds email sign in, database tooling, example screens and environment setup. Premium adds a Stripe checkout starter, email sending, tests, an automated pipeline and a walkthrough call for your developers.

A starter is a base, so it will not contain your business logic. Your team or ours builds that on top.

## What to do, and what to avoid

**Do:**
- Choose the stack your team can maintain, not the most fashionable one.
- List the services you already know you will use.
- Have a developer read the README and run the kit on a fresh machine.
- Remove example screens you do not need.
- Keep dependencies updated on a schedule.

**Avoid:**
- Adding every possible library "just in case".
- Starting features before the kit runs cleanly for everyone.
- Committing secrets to the repository.
- Copying a kit from the internet that nobody understands.
- Skipping the checks that run on each change.

## Who this is for

This service suits an agency that starts many similar projects and wants one dependable base. It suits a founder about to hire their first developer and wants the project set up properly. It also suits a team moving to Next.js that wants a reference setup before building.

## What we need from you

Send your preferred stack, your hosting choice and a short list of services to include. Share a repository you own and add us as a collaborator. We never need your passwords. After you order, we send a short checklist and keep you updated until the kit is deployed and documented.
